Less Travel, More Training: Luis Robles Rethinks U.S. Youth Soccer Share page Soccer Interview Less Travel, More Training: Luis Robles Rethinks U.S. Youth Soccer Zach Lowy Soccer Reporter Fact checked by: Sergey Demidov Updated: Oct 30, 2026, 6:01 PM Published: Oct 30, 2026, 11:59 AM Editorial Standards Why Trust Us? Former U.S. international goalkeeper Luis Robles, now a top executive at MLS NEXT, tells RG how one overlooked New Jersey teenager became a Red Bull New York academy player, why the league requires a full scholarship at every club and why four training sessions for every match matter more than cross-country tournaments. (Photo by Dustin Satloff/Getty Images) An hour can make all the difference between a promising young soccer player and a future professional. For one youngster in New Jersey, it nearly cost him the opportunity to fulfill his potential. While watching his son's team train, former United States international goalkeeper Luis Robles spotted an exceptional player. But there was a problem: the youngster lived an hour away, and his family struggled to afford the journey. Rather than allowing those circumstances to dictate his future, Robles and the club found a solution. “My son is on one of the top MLS teams in New Jersey. I went to a training session, and there was a kid who was exceptional. I said to the parents, ‘We’ve got to bring him; he’s got to try out,’ but then I found out it was an hour drive for his family, and it was hard for them to both carve out the time and afford it,” Robles said in an exclusive RG interview. “The club found a way for that kid to play on that team and create resources for that kid. That club wants to win; they pride themselves on being one of the top clubs. If it meant that they had to do a scholarship for the kid, then that’s what they did; the kid didn’t pay a dime to play last year. When we had to go to Arizona, the parents found a way for the kid to go, because the parents want to win.” “We’re talking about a player that was not even in MLS NEXT, that wasn’t on a roster, who was seen … that kind of thing did not exist during my playing experience. There are now eyeballs everywhere, and there are parents who want to win everywhere. They brought that kid to training, and the coach said, ‘We need him.’ The academy director says, ‘We’ll figure it out.’ He ends up being one of our most important players. We play New York City FC; we’re losing 2-0, he sets up the 2-1 goal, and he scores the equalizer. He gets moved up to the U15s, they win the cup and the national championship, and he now plays for Red Bull New York. There are dozens of those examples now, and that’s progress.” Scholarships And A Wider Funnel The youngster's journey from an overlooked prospect to the Red Bulls' academy encapsulates the challenge facing American youth soccer: identifying talent is one thing, but ensuring players have the resources to fulfill their potential is another. Since replacing the U.S. Soccer Development Academy in 2020, MLS NEXT has grown into a nationwide network of more than 53,000 players , with its Academy Division widening access to the national development pathway. But with that expansion comes a fundamental question: is it better to provide 50,000 youngsters with competitive opportunities, or concentrate resources on producing the next 500 American stars? “I think our responsibility is to give those 50,000 players the best experience possible within our control. That's having a standards-based environment where they get good coaching, they get good competition, and we keep the cost down. The ones that really rise up to the next level don't have the means to get there, because we have a rule that there has to be a full scholarship in every NEXT club. But even when we created the rule, we did an evaluation where clubs were already doing it. There's room for us to crank that thing up, and our clubs are already doing it, because it's within the American spirit, which is a competitive spirit that wants to win.” “One of the questions that has to be asked is: what are we accessing? Are we accessing the top level, or just creating access to soccer? If it is just creating access for soccer, this is why it's so important to launch the Academy Division, because we're in more clubs, and we are widening the funnel. When one of those players has the ability to play in one of those clubs, and they go to one of these events, we're hoping they get exposure, but also, with the standards that we're promoting with this idea of it's all built around the player, we're also hoping that they're put in environments where they excel. Are there clubs around them that they can be a part of, which then gives them accessibility to NEXT and the player development pathway? Or is it the child that really is challenged socioeconomically and is really good?” An Unlikely Road To The Pros (Photo by Dustin Satloff/Getty Images) Robles himself knows how unpredictable the road to professional soccer can be. Born in Fort Huachuca, Arizona, to a Puerto Rican father and a Korean mother, Robles grew up far from the country's traditional soccer hotbeds. After recording a school-record 346 saves at the University of Portland, he was selected by D.C. United with the 50th overall pick in the 2007 MLS SuperDraft. Rather than beginning his professional career in MLS, however, Robles crossed the Atlantic to join Kaiserslautern in January 2007. He made his league debut in October 2008 before eventually becoming the club's starting goalkeeper following an injury to Tobias Sippel. After missing the start of preseason due to his involvement at the 2009 CONCACAF Gold Cup, Robles lost his starting position as the Red Devils secured promotion to the Bundesliga. This, combined with the emergence of young goalkeeper Kevin Trapp, saw Robles trade Kaiserslautern for second-tier Karlsruher SC, establishing himself as the No. 1 before losing his place and being released. By 2012, Robles feared his playing days were over. A proposed move to the Vancouver Whitecaps had fallen through, leaving the 28-year-old searching for employment and health insurance for his pregnant wife. He even took a job as a real estate agent before contacting MLS executive Ali Curtis, who helped facilitate his return to professional soccer through the Allocation Draft. It ended up saving his career. Robles joined the New York Red Bulls, still one of the most closely watched clubs in New York sports betting , and seized his opportunity following an injury to starting goalkeeper Ryan Meara. He went on to set an MLS record of 183 consecutive appearances and helped the club win three Supporters' Shields in 2013, 2015 and 2018. After departing as the club’s all-time appearance leader, Robles spent the 2020 season with Inter Miami, now a headline team at Florida sportsbooks , before announcing his retirement on Jan. 6, 2021. He then joined MLS NEXT as senior manager of programming before being promoted to technical director in March 2024 and vice president and general manager two years later. Curtis, meanwhile, became president of MLS NEXT Pro and executive vice president of MLS Sporting Development. Luis Robles And MLS NEXT By The Numbers 53,000+ MLS NEXT Players The nationwide network has grown that large since replacing the U.S. Soccer Development Academy in 2020. Statistics 1 Full Scholarship Per Club MLS NEXT requires a full scholarship at every club so top players without the means can still rise. Statistics 4 Training Sessions Per Match That is the ratio Robles calls ideal for player development, or three to one at younger ages. Statistics 183 Straight MLS Appearances Robles set the league record with the Red Bulls and won three Supporters' Shields with the club. Statistics 346 Saves At Portland Robles set the school record before D.C. United drafted him 50th overall in 2007. Statistics Four Training Sessions For Every Match Having experienced the uncertainty of pursuing a professional career abroad, Robles is now helping shape a domestic development pathway designed to provide young Americans with more opportunities closer to home, ensuring that they don’t have to move to Germany to receive a world-class soccer education. “MLS NEXT is built on player development. The ideal ratio for optimal player development is four training sessions to one match. Depending on the age, if it's younger, it's three to one. We want to balance the ratio, because it's in training that these players improve. The match is where they show the results. They show all that they've been working on, and if we can minimize double fixtures. The right group of players in the right environment with a good coach against good competition, you apply that week in and week out over a period of time, and players are going to develop. Players are going to get better, and so this is at least some of the pillars and the framework that guides NEXT and what we're trying to do.” For Robles, improving American youth soccer means challenging the assumption that more matches, tournaments and travel necessarily produce better players. Rather than prioritizing short-term results, MLS NEXT is emphasizing consistent training, meaningful competition and long-term development. The emphasis on training rather than results is reflected in MLS NEXT's competition rules. At the U13 level, players on matchday rosters are generally required to receive at least one uninterrupted 25-minute period, ensuring that youngsters have meaningful opportunities to develop rather than spending entire matches on the sidelines. Why MLS NEXT Fest Brings Everyone To One Place It also means reconsidering how frequently families are expected to travel across the country. Through events such as MLS NEXT Fest, the organization aims to concentrate national competition and scouting opportunities into a smaller number of showcases, allowing players to test themselves against unfamiliar opponents without committing to a relentless tournament schedule. “Why would a family go to Fest? Depending on your age group, it may just be to get top competition. If you're in the U13 and U16 groups, those are really college identification age groups. I'm going to go out there because I'm going to play a team if I'm based out of New Jersey; I'm going to play a team in Michigan, in California, in Texas, and that's a good experience, because it only happens maybe once a year. If you're in the U17s and U19s, the reason why we have a Nashville event as opposed to regionals is that if we can gather as many college coaches in one place as possible, the chances of a player being exposed go up. If we did regional events in New Jersey, it's going to be Northeast schools. If we do it in Southern California, it's going to be Western schools.” “But if we're doing it in one spot, not only do we have an aggregation which makes for better competition, but we have an aggregation which makes for better scouting. It helps with international team, with MLS Academy scouting, and with college scouting. We have one annual event that's called MLS NEXT Fest, and the reason why we only have one optional event is that we don't want to burden families with a bunch of events. We don't want to make it feel like they have to go and do this and this and that.” “The other two events are by qualification: that's basically the group stage of the World Cup, where you play three games in four days, and then if you make it through that, you go to the Cup. There's a competition element, but of course, there's college recruiting, and there's scouting. In the academy division, which we launched last year, there are 10 Cup qualifiers, and the idea with that is that no one flies. The idea is that people don't have to stay in hotels, but there's going to be some variety and competition; if you do well there, then you go to Cup, which is where the homegrown division will also be competing.” Educating Families On Player Development For Robles, these modifications are part of a broader effort to educate families about what effective player development actually entails. While national tournaments and international showcases can provide valuable experiences, he believes that a consistent training environment, qualified coaching and appropriate competition are ultimately more important than the number of events a youngster attends. “We don't talk directly to families or players; we speak with the clubs. I think part of our responsibility is also getting more education awareness out to families of what optimal player development looks like. It doesn't mean that you go to Spain three times for international tournaments, or that you fill up every other weekend with the tournaments, or that you're going to 17 different talent IDs.” “It means that you find the right environment with the right group of players of like mind, with a good coach, that has good training, and over the course of time, if you put in the work, these are the pillars of development. They want to win and develop players, and they'll go find those players, and they'll figure out how they can get access to it. Even this past weekend, we had a talent ID event where we invited players outside of NEXT; they got free gear, and they were at MLS Academies. And the hope is that they get exposure and that they can take the next step somewhere else.” Zach Lowy Soccer Reporter

Zach Lowy is a seasoned freelance football journalist with more than a decade of experience writing for top-tier news outlets. His expertise and insights have also made him a sought-after guest on radio and television, including appearances on BBC, SiriusXMFC, and other prominent sports platforms.

Before joining RG, Zach contributed to well-known sports websites, including FotMob (2024–present), BetUS (2023–present), and BET Central (2019–2024), where he built a strong reputation for in-depth analysis and compelling storytelling.

A graduate of George Washington University with a degree in global sports journalism, Zach leverages his multilingual skills to conduct interviews and report in both Spanish and Portuguese. This linguistic ability has enabled him to engage directly with major football figures and cover prestigious tournaments, such as the 2016 Copa América and the 2018 FIFA World Cup.

Throughout his career, Zach has interviewed legendary players such as Simão Sabrosa and Diego Forlán and tackled a broad spectrum of football topics — from Marseille’s historic match-fixing scandal to the rapid rise of Joan García with Espanyol. His trilingual fluency and sharp focus on football make him a versatile and insightful voice in the sport.

Zach is based in Washington, D.C., where he continues to cover global football stories and share his passion for the beautiful game.
